quickAnswer: Hopkinton has the highest share of homes built since 2010 of the 50 towns we serve (20.4%), and one of the lowest shares built before 1980 (35.1%). Newer houses can be tighter, so sizing and ventilation deserve attention.
body: ## The newest housing stock in MetroWest

Of the 50 towns we serve, Hopkinton ranks first for homes built since 2010. The Census Bureau's 2022 American Community Survey (ACS) counts 1,431 of its 7,008 housing units in that group, a 20.4% share, against 8.4% for the middle town. The median Hopkinton home dates from 1990, against 1975 for the middle town. Homes built before 1980 total 2,463 (35.1%), which puts the town 49th of 50 on that measure.
The town's own history fits. Wikipedia describes the town's population growth rate as faster than any other municipality in the commonwealth. The 1,431 homes built since 2010 fit that picture.
## What a new house asks of its equipment

A house built in recent years can have better insulation, tighter windows and ducts run inside the building envelope. That is good news for energy use, and it changes the job. Equipment sized for an old, leaky house is too big for a tight one. An oversized furnace or air conditioner short-cycles, wears faster and does a poor job of controlling humidity.

So the heating load gets assessed before any system is quoted. A straight swap of the old model can be the wrong answer even in a recent house, since equipment chosen at construction may not suit the finished home.

Tight houses also need fresh air. Without ventilation, moisture, cooking fumes and chemical off-gassing from new furnishings stay inside. Stuffiness or window condensation in a tight house is a reason to ask about ventilation and humidity control.
## Still, not everything is new: oil, villages and historic districts

Newer does not mean no oil. Utility gas heats 3,788 occupied homes (56.8%), but fuel oil or kerosene still heats 2,206 (33.1%), 27th of 50. Electricity heats only 378 homes (5.7%), 47th of 50. Bottled or tank gas heats 194 homes, and wood 108.

The older part of town is distinctive too. Hopkinton was incorporated on December 13, 1715, and 215 properties are listed in the State Register of Historic Places. Twenty-three properties sit in the Hopkinton Center Historic District around the Town Common, and ninety-seven sit in the Woodville Historic District, established in 2005. Wikipedia describes former factory worker housing in the center of town, contrasted against the more rural areas around it. Older village houses and recent houses need very different work. A historic frame may call for ductless heads and hot-water radiators. A recent house needs a precise load calculation and perhaps a ventilation upgrade.
## The first Hopkinton fact most people know

Hopkinton has hosted the start of the Boston Marathon since 1924, and it is a sister city of Marathon, Greece. Hopkinton sits in the southwestern corner of Middlesex County, 26 miles west of Boston and 17 miles east of Worcester, and is bordered by six towns including Milford, where Mass HVAC is based. The building fact that matters is more ordinary: 1,431 homes were built since 2010, so a large share of the town's housing is recent.
## Rebates when the utility is unconfirmed

Our records do not confirm Hopkinton's electric utility, so any heat pump rebate depends on the company that serves your address. The 2,234 homes built in 2000 or later are the ones most likely to clear the weatherization step. Details are on the [heat pump page](/cities/hopkinton/heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits).

faq.q: My Hopkinton house is only about ten years old. Do I still need to think about sizing?
faq.a: Yes. A newer house is tighter, so it may need less heating and cooling capacity than an older house of the same size. Oversized equipment short-cycles and handles humidity poorly. With 20.4% of Hopkinton homes built since 2010, a load check is worth doing before any replacement. The load check also decides whether a modulating unit is worth considering.

faq.q: Do newer homes qualify for the whole-home heat pump rebate?
faq.a: Houses from 2000 on skip the assessment step of the weatherization test, which covers 2,234 Hopkinton homes. Everything else still has to line up: an eligible installer, equipment installed in 2026 and a participating utility. Rebates run through the utility serving your address, so confirm at masssave.com.

faq.q: Is Hopkinton mostly gas or oil?
faq.a: Both. Utility gas heats 3,788 occupied homes (56.8%, 13th of 50) and fuel oil heats 2,206 (33.1%, 27th), against medians of 41.9% and 36.5%. Which applies to you depends on your street and your house. We check what is available at the estimate, and a heat pump is the third option for either group.

faq.q: Do historic-district houses in Hopkinton need special equipment?
faq.a: Not special, but careful. Old frames and plaster limit where ducts and pipes go, and exterior equipment may be subject to local review. Ask the town about district rules before choosing. Ductless heads often fit where ducts cannot.

heating-installation-repair.quickAnswer: Hopkinton heats mostly with utility gas (56.8%) and oil (33.1%), in a town where the median home dates from 1990. Newer houses are tight, so a furnace or boiler should be sized from the actual load, not copied from the old nameplate.
body: ## Heat for houses built after 1990

The median Hopkinton home was built in 1990, and 1,431 were built since 2010. Equipment in those houses is not ancient, but it is not immortal either. Furnaces from the 1990s are old enough that heat exchangers can crack, igniters can fail and boards can give out.
### Oversizing is a common mistake

A tight house with a furnace that is too large gets hot fast, the burner shuts off, and the cycle repeats. Temperatures swing and the equipment wears early. A load calculation using the real walls, windows and ducts fixes this.
### Gas, oil and conversion

- Gas homes (3,788) are the straightforward case: replace like for like with a correctly sized unit.
- Oil homes (2,206) face a three-way choice: another oil unit, a gas conversion where a main reaches the street, or a heat pump.
- Tank gas (194) and wood (108) homes may want a system that is easier to supply.
- Electric homes are few (378), but they may gain from a heat pump.
### Two-stage and modulating equipment

Newer houses can suit furnaces and boilers that adjust their output instead of running flat out. They hold temperature more evenly. Whether the extra cost pays off depends on the house, and we say so.
### Older Hopkinton homes

Not every house is new: 750 homes date from 1939 or earlier. Older houses with radiators call for more traditional work: boiler replacement, pipe repair and care around original materials. Historic districts may have exterior rules for vents and equipment, so ask the town first.
### Permits

Gas equipment swaps need a permit and a final inspection by the town, and Massachusetts allows only licensed plumbers or gas fitters to pull the gas permit. Ask the building department how Hopkinton handles it before the work is scheduled.
### Few old houses, many from 1980 on

Hopkinton ranks 49th of 50 for homes built before 1980 (35.1%) and has 2,311 homes from 1980 to 1999 plus 2,234 from 2000 on. That puts most of the town's replacement work in houses from the 1980s or later, so a load assessment is usually the first step.
### Emergencies

If the heat fails, call (508) 786-8755 at any hour. January in Hopkinton averages a low of 20 F and a high of 40 F, and snowfall averages around 45 inches, so a dead system in midwinter is worth treating as urgent. A free written estimate comes before work starts.

faq.q: My Hopkinton furnace is getting old. Should I replace it?
faq.a: Not automatically. If it runs well and passes a safety check, keep it. A cracked heat exchanger or repeated failures point to replacement, and we will show you the evidence. With the median home built in 1990, many furnaces here are old enough to be worth an inspection before the next cold snap.

faq.q: Is a modulating furnace worth it in a new house?
faq.a: It can be, because tight houses benefit from steady output. The gain depends on the ducts and the load, so we compare options at the estimate. Hopkinton has 1,431 homes built since 2010, the highest share of the 50 towns we serve, so this is a question we expect to hear often.

faq.q: Should I switch from oil to gas in Hopkinton?
faq.a: Only if a gas main reaches your street. Fuel oil heats 2,206 occupied homes here (33.1%), and utility gas heats 3,788 (56.8%), so both fuels are common. A conversion adds piping and a permit, and a heat pump is the third option. We compare the three for your house at the estimate.

air-conditioning-installation-repair.quickAnswer: Hopkinton is 69.7% detached houses and 14.6% townhouse-style homes, with a median build year of 1990, so cooling work is often about what is already installed. Oversizing, aging units and upstairs hot spots are what we check first.
body: ## Cooling homes that were built to take central air

Hopkinton has 4,882 detached houses and 1,023 attached homes, and 2,311 homes date from 1980 to 1999 and 2,234 from 2000 on. Newer houses are more likely to have ductwork already in place, so the cooling question may be about what is installed rather than whether anything can be.
### First-generation units are aging

Condensers installed in the 1990s and early 2000s may be due for replacement. Signs include longer run times, ice on the coil, a unit that trips its breaker and rising bills. A newer unit with a variable-speed compressor can be quieter and handle humidity better.
### Oversized units in tight houses

A tight house can need less cooling than the same floor area did in the past. An oversized unit cools fast, cuts out and leaves the air damp. We size from the load, including windows facing the afternoon sun and any rooms over garages.
### Second floors and bonus rooms

- A bonus room over a garage often runs hot.
- A second thermostat or zone can balance a two-story house.
- A ductless head can fix one stubborn room without touching the ducts.
- Return air upstairs makes a surprising difference.
### Townhouses and condos

With 773 homes in buildings with 5 or more units and 222 in buildings with 3 or 4 units, there are many shared-wall homes. Equipment location is often limited by association rules, so quiet operation and a compact condenser matter.
### Heat pumps for both seasons
One heat pump can do both jobs, which suits a newer house that needs both. Our [heat pump page](/cities/hopkinton/heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits) covers the rebate rules.
### Repair or replace
Capacitors, contactors and fan motors are routine repairs. A compressor failure or refrigerant leak on an old unit often points to replacement.
### Hopkinton summers

The town's summers tend to be hot and humid, with daily highs averaging in the 80s and readings in the 90s between June and August. July averages a low of 65 F and a high of 84 F. Those figures are why the humidity side of cooling matters as much as the temperature side.

faq.q: Why does one room in my newer Hopkinton house stay hot?
faq.a: It is often a duct issue: a long run, a pinched flex duct or no return. Sometimes the room is simply over a garage. A technician can test airflow, and a ductless head can solve what ducts cannot.

faq.q: How long do central air conditioners usually last?
faq.a: Many last well over a decade, though it depends on maintenance and conditions. Rising bills and frequent repairs signal that it is time to plan. With 2,234 Hopkinton homes built since 2000 and 2,311 from 1980 to 1999, a lot of central air units here are in their middle or later years.

faq.q: Can I cool a Hopkinton townhouse or condo with a ductless system?
faq.a: Often, yes. Hopkinton has 1,023 attached homes (14.6%) and 773 homes in buildings with 5 or more units, where outdoor space is limited and association rules may apply. A compact condenser with one or two indoor heads suits that setting, and the layout is chosen after we see the unit and its outdoor location.

heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits.quickAnswer: Hopkinton's utility is not confirmed in our records, so the rebate depends on the utility serving your address. Of 6,674 occupied homes, 2,206 burn oil and 194 use tank gas, and 2,234 homes were built in 2000 or later.
body: ## A head start on the rebate rules

Mass Save's whole-home rebate in 2026 is $2,650 per ton, up to $8,500 per home, and the home must be weatherized first. Homes built in 2000 or later meet that test on age. Everything else is on our [main heat pump page](/services/heat-pumps-ductless-mini-splits).
### Who is the utility?

We have not confirmed which utility serves Hopkinton, so your electric bill is the first stop. If a municipal utility turns out to serve your street, the gas-heat condition changes who qualifies, and the municipal program applies to the rest.
### Who gains the most

Oil is the target. Hopkinton has 2,206 oil homes, 27th of 50, and a tight newer house can need less capacity from a heat pump. Tank-gas homes (194) and the 378 electric-heat homes may also gain from a more efficient source of warmth. Gas homes (3,788) need a closer comparison.
### Keep the boiler or not
A whole-home system aims to carry the full load. A partial-home system keeps the old furnace or boiler for the coldest days.
### Ducted or ductless

Newer houses often have good ducts, so a ducted air handler can reuse them. Additions and bonus rooms may suit ductless heads. See the [cooling page](/cities/hopkinton/air-conditioning-installation-repair) for the layout issues.
### Historic homes
Older houses in historic districts such as Hopkinton Center and Woodville can lack usable ducts. Ductless heads avoid cutting into old plaster, though exterior unit placement may need local review.
### Age bands and the 2000 line

Hopkinton has 2,234 homes built in 2000 or later (31.9%), including 1,431 since 2010, which is 20.4% and the highest share in the group. The other bands are 750 homes from 1939 or earlier, 561 from 1940 to 1959, 1,152 from 1960 to 1979 and 2,311 from 1980 to 1999. About a third of the town's housing is therefore ready on age, and the rest starts with an assessment.
### Climate for sizing

January in Hopkinton averages 20 F at night and 40 F in the afternoon, with snowfall around 45 inches. A cold-climate heat pump is sized against that winter, not against the summer cooling load, which is why the heating load comes first.

faq.q: Does a 2005 Hopkinton house pass the weatherization test?
faq.a: Yes. A home built in 2000 or later meets the condition without an assessment. You still need an eligible installer, a participating utility and equipment installed in 2026. Hopkinton has 2,234 homes in that age group, so a large part of the town can skip the assessment step entirely.

faq.q: Is a heat pump a good choice if I heat with gas?
faq.a: It can be, especially if you also want cooling, but gas is often cheaper per unit of heat. Gas heats 56.8% of occupied Hopkinton homes, 13th of 50, so many owners face this question. A partial-home setup is one way to use both. We compare options for your house.

faq.q: Which utility pays the rebate in Hopkinton?
faq.a: It depends on who serves your address, so check your electric bill. Then confirm program terms at masssave.com, since they can change. Only 378 Hopkinton homes (5.7%) heat with electricity today, 47th of 50, so for most households the utility question comes up for the first time with a heat pump.

hvac-maintenance-tune-ups.quickAnswer: With 33.1% of Hopkinton homes on oil and a large share of recent construction, maintenance means two different jobs: yearly cleaning for oil burners and early checks on young equipment before small faults grow.
body: ## Maintenance for young equipment and old burners

Hopkinton has two maintenance worlds. In older houses and the 2,206 oil-heated homes, an annual cleaning is basic: burner, nozzle, filter and combustion test. In newer houses, equipment is more likely to be young, and the job is to catch small faults early.
### What can go wrong in young systems

- Clogged filters in tight houses that circulate the same air.
- Condensate drains that block and leak onto ceilings.
- Loose electrical connections that cause weak starts.
- Refrigerant leaks that show up as long run times.
- Coils coated with construction dust from the first year.
### Why new does not mean care-free
New equipment still needs upkeep, and manufacturers may expect it to be done. Without a record of service, a claim can be harder to make. Check your equipment's paperwork for what it requires.
### The first replacement cycle

With 1,431 houses built since 2010, plenty of equipment is still young. A tune-up shows how much life is left, so replacement can be planned for spring or fall rather than forced during a heat wave or cold snap.
### Seasonal schedule

- **Late summer:** heating checks, including the oil burner.
- **Spring:** cooling and mini-split checks.
- **Any time:** noises, odors or short cycling.
### Owners and renters
Renters make up 12.9% of households. Landlords who service equipment before winter can avoid cold-night calls, and tenants should report problems in writing.

### Keeping a record
A service record that notes the fuel, the age of the equipment from the nameplate and anything likely to need attention in the next season is useful. Keeping that record in one place helps when you sell the house, when a new owner asks about the system, or when you compare a repair quote with a replacement.
### What the climate asks of equipment

Average temperatures run from 20 to 40 F in January and from 65 to 84 F in July, and daily highs can reach the 90s between June and August. Heating gear works hard in one season and cooling gear in another, so a spring visit and a late-summer visit each have a job. Annual precipitation of 51.25 inches also keeps outdoor units exposed to damp.
### Easy things you can do
Keep outdoor units clear and check the thermostat batteries. Read the [heating page](/cities/hopkinton/heating-installation-repair) if a repair turns into a replacement decision.

faq.q: Do newer Hopkinton homes really need annual service?
faq.a: Yes, though there is usually less to do. Filters, drains, coils and controls still need attention, and manufacturers may expect a record of upkeep. Hopkinton has 1,431 homes built since 2010, so a large block of equipment is young and a yearly check is how small faults get found before they grow.

faq.q: When is the best time for an oil burner cleaning?
faq.a: Late summer or early fall, before heating season. Once a year is the usual advice. Oil heats 2,206 Hopkinton homes (33.1%).

faq.q: Should a landlord schedule the heating check in a Hopkinton rental?
faq.a: Yes, ahead of winter. Renters make up 12.9% of Hopkinton households (858), and 773 homes sit in buildings of five or more units, where one system can serve several households. A check in late summer is easier to arrange than an emergency in January, and tenants should report problems to the landlord in writing.

indoor-air-quality.quickAnswer: Hopkinton's tight new houses (20.4% built since 2010) can trap moisture, fumes and particles unless ventilation works. Older homes can leak instead. We start with the house type and fix ventilation, humidity and filtration in that order.
body: ## Tight houses need a way to breathe

Newer homes tend to be built to keep outdoor air out. That reduces drafts and energy use, and it also means anything produced inside stays inside. Cooking, showers, cleaning products, pets and new furniture add moisture and chemicals that a leaky house would have let out.
### Signs of a house that is too tight

- Condensation on windows in winter.
- Cooking smells that linger.
- A stuffy feeling in bedrooms overnight.
- Mold on bathroom ceilings.
### What helps

A bathroom fan that vents outside and actually runs, a range hood that exhausts, and a ventilator that brings in filtered fresh air. Heat recovery ventilators exchange air while keeping most of the heat. We can recommend what fits your ducts.
### Humidity

Winter air is dry, and humidifiers can help comfort, but keep the level moderate. Summer humidity is handled by correctly sized cooling or a dehumidifier. Oversized equipment is a common cause of clammy rooms.
### Older houses in the villages

Hopkinton has 750 homes dating from 1939 or earlier, and older houses can behave the opposite way. They tend to leak air, which brings in dust and pollen, and basements can be damp. Old materials matter if you plan renovations, so have a qualified specialist test before work begins.
### Filters and ducts
Better filters help if the system can pull air through them. Duct cleaning is worth considering after building work, when leftover dust may be in the ducts, or when an inspection finds damage.
### Rain, ponds and damp air

Hopkinton averages 51.25 inches of precipitation a year, spread fairly evenly through the year, with November the wettest month at 4.69 inches. The town also has 1.6 square miles of water, including Whitehall Reservoir and Hopkinton Reservoir. In a house with a basement, steady outdoor moisture is a reason to watch humidity all year, not only in summer.
### Newer is not the same as ventilated

With 1,431 homes built since 2010 (20.4%, first of 50) and 2,234 since 2000, the stock is among the newest we serve. A bathroom fan that vents outdoors and a range hood that exhausts are the simplest checks in any of them.
### Testing

A test records humidity, particles or carbon monoxide on the day it is taken, so the result lasts only if the source is fixed. See our [maintenance page](/cities/hopkinton/hvac-maintenance-tune-ups) for filter schedules.

faq.q: Why are my windows foggy in a newer house?
faq.a: Moisture is staying inside. Run bathroom fans, use the range hood, and consider a ventilator or a lower humidifier setting. Persistent fog suggests a ventilation problem. Hopkinton has 1,431 homes built since 2010, and construction of that era tends to be tight, so fogging is a common sign that the air is not changing enough.

faq.q: Do I need duct cleaning after building work?
faq.a: Often, yes, if dust got into the ducts. Inspect first, and seal vents during future work. If the house is one of the 2,234 built in 2000 or later, leftover construction dust can be part of the picture, and a visual check of the ducts tells us whether cleaning is worth the cost.

faq.q: Do Hopkinton's older village houses need different air fixes?
faq.a: Often. The 750 homes from 1939 or earlier tend to leak air, so dust, pollen and damp basements are the usual complaints. Woodville and the center have historic districts, so exterior work may need local review. Sealing and moisture control usually come before filtration or ventilation equipment in a house that old.
